topic: Uses and applications of electromagnetic waves
subject: physics

items.q: The specification lists a practical application for each group of electromagnetic waves. Which pairing is correct?
items.correct: Fibre optic communications use visible light
items.misconception: Satellite communication uses radio waves
items.why: Radio waves are introduced as the waves used for broadcasting over long distances, and everyday speech calls any transmitted signal a 'radio signal', so satellites are assumed to use them as well. The specification pairs radio waves with television and radio, and microwaves with satellite communications. Microwaves are used because they pass through the atmosphere to the satellite; many radio waves are reflected or absorbed instead.
items.random_wrong: Sun tanning lamps mainly give out infrared

items.q: Which use does the specification give for radio waves?
items.correct: Broadcasting television and radio programmes
items.misconception: Sending signals to and from satellites in orbit
items.why: Radio waves are introduced as the waves used for broadcasting over long distances, and everyday speech calls any transmitted signal a 'radio signal', so satellites are assumed to use them as well. The specification pairs radio waves with television and radio, and microwaves with satellite communications. Microwaves are used because they pass through the atmosphere to the satellite; many radio waves are reflected or absorbed instead.
items.random_wrong: Carrying signals along fibre optic cables

items.q: A signal is sent from a ground station up to a satellite in orbit and then back down to a second ground station. Which waves carry the signal?
items.correct: Microwaves, which pass through the atmosphere
items.misconception: Radio waves, which are used for broadcasting today
items.why: Radio waves are introduced as the waves used for broadcasting over long distances, and everyday speech calls any transmitted signal a 'radio signal', so satellites are assumed to use them as well. The specification pairs radio waves with television and radio, and microwaves with satellite communications. Microwaves are used because they pass through the atmosphere to the satellite; many radio waves are reflected or absorbed instead.
items.random_wrong: Infrared, which is given out by all hot objects

items.q: How does a microwave oven cook food?
items.correct: The food absorbs microwaves and heats up
items.misconception: Microwaves heat the middle of the food first
items.why: The phrase 'cooks from the inside out' is repeated so often that students take it literally, and it seems to explain why microwaved food can be hot in the middle and cool at the edges – which is really uneven absorption and uneven spreading of energy. Microwaves are absorbed mainly in the outer few centimetres of the food, and energy spreads inwards by conduction. A microwave oven is faster than a grill because energy is delivered throughout that outer layer rather than only to the surface, not because heating starts in the centre.
items.random_wrong: Microwaves make the food slightly radioactive

items.q: An electric grill glows red and cooks the food placed underneath it. Which radiation transfers energy to the food?
items.correct: Infrared, which is absorbed by the food surface
items.misconception: Microwaves, because all cookers use microwaves
items.why: The microwave oven is the cooking application students meet in this topic, so 'microwaves cook food' is generalised to every cooker. The specification lists cooking food under both microwaves and infrared. A glowing element emits infrared, which the surface of the food absorbs; a microwave oven emits microwaves, which penetrate a few centimetres before being absorbed.
items.random_wrong: Ultraviolet, because the element glows white

items.q: An infrared camera is used to find a person standing in a dark field at night. Why does the person show up on the image?
items.correct: Their body gives out infrared that the camera detects
items.misconception: The camera shines visible light on the person
items.why: Every camera students have used needs light, and a flash is the obvious way to photograph in the dark, so an emitter is assumed rather than a detector. All objects emit infrared, and warmer objects emit more. An infrared camera forms an image from that emitted radiation, which is why a person shows up in complete darkness and why the image shows the warm and cool parts of an object.
items.random_wrong: Infrared from the body can be seen by the eye too

items.q: Which type of electromagnetic wave carries the signals in a fibre optic cable?
items.correct: Visible light, sent as very rapid pulses
items.misconception: Microwaves, as used for satellite phone links
items.why: Students group all communications together and reach for the waves already labelled 'communication waves', without noticing that the specification lists a separate application for visible light. The specification pairs visible light with fibre optic communications. The signal is a rapid train of light pulses travelling along a thin glass fibre, which is why the fibre is transparent rather than metal.
items.random_wrong: Radio waves, as used for television aerials

items.q: A sunbed is used to give a tan. Which statement about the radiation it uses is correct?
items.correct: It gives out ultraviolet, which can harm skin
items.misconception: It gives out infrared, and the heat browns skin
items.why: Sunbathing feels hot, and heat is the sensation students associate with a tan, so the tan is credited to infrared rather than to the radiation that cannot be felt at all. The specification pairs sun tanning with ultraviolet. Ultraviolet is absorbed by skin cells and causes them to produce more pigment; it can also damage those cells. Infrared warms the skin but does not tan it.
items.random_wrong: It gives out visible light, which the skin absorbs

items.q: Why does a broken bone show up clearly on an X-ray photograph?
items.correct: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone
items.misconception: X-rays pass through bone but are absorbed by flesh
items.why: The bone appears white and bright on the image, and students read 'bright' as 'the radiation arrived here', which reverses what actually happened. Bone contains heavier elements and absorbs X-rays strongly, so few reach the detector behind it and a shadow is formed. The image is a shadow picture: pale where absorption was greatest.
items.random_wrong: X-rays are reflected from the surface of the bone

items.q: Gamma rays are used in hospitals to treat cancer. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: A beam of gamma rays is aimed at the tumour to kill cells
items.misconception: Gamma rays leave the treated tissue permanently radioactive
items.why: Irradiation and contamination are easily confused, and gamma rays come from radioactive sources, so students assume the radioactivity is passed on. Radioactivity is a property of unstable nuclei. Gamma rays transfer energy to the cells they pass through, damaging them, but they do not turn stable nuclei into unstable ones.
items.random_wrong: Gamma rays are far too dangerous ever to be used here

items.q: (HT only) Explain why microwaves rather than infrared are used to send signals to a communications satellite.
items.correct: Microwaves pass through the atmosphere, infrared does not
items.misconception: Microwaves travel much faster through space than infrared can
items.why: Higher frequency is read as 'more energetic', and 'more energetic' slides into 'faster', especially when the spectrum is drawn as a sequence from weak to strong. The electromagnetic spectrum is a continuous range of waves that all transfer energy at the same speed through a vacuum. Microwaves are chosen for satellite links because the atmosphere lets them through, not because they arrive sooner.
items.random_wrong: Infrared cannot cross the vacuum of space, but microwaves do

items.q: (HT only) An energy efficient lamp produces ultraviolet inside its tube, yet the room is lit by visible light. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: A coating absorbs ultraviolet and emits visible light
items.misconception: The lamp is designed to send ultraviolet into the room
items.why: The specification pairs ultraviolet with energy efficient lamps, and students read the pairing as 'what comes out' rather than 'what is used inside'. Ultraviolet is a step in how the lamp works, not its output. The coating on the inside of the tube absorbs ultraviolet and re-emits visible light, so the room is lit by visible light.
items.random_wrong: The ultraviolet itself is the light you see the room by

items.q: Food that has been in a microwave oven is slightly radioactive afterwards.
items.correct: The food absorbs microwaves and its temperature rises; nothing about the food becomes radioactive.
items.misconception: 'Radiation' from the oven makes the food radioactive.
items.why: The single word 'radiation' is used for electromagnetic waves and for nuclear radiation, so students transfer everything they know about the second to the first. Microwaves are part of the electromagnetic spectrum. Absorbing them raises the energy store of the food, exactly as absorbing infrared from a grill does. Only processes that change the nuclei of atoms can make something radioactive, and microwaves cannot do that.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Ultraviolet is the light you see coming out of a lamp.
items.correct: Ultraviolet cannot be seen by the human eye; it lies just beyond the violet end of the visible spectrum.
items.misconception: Ultraviolet is a kind of visible light, so a glowing lamp is shining ultraviolet at you.
items.why: The name contains 'violet', and ultraviolet is drawn on spectrum diagrams right next to the coloured band, so students place it inside the visible range. The visible spectrum ends at violet. Ultraviolet has a shorter wavelength than any colour the eye can detect, which is why the ultraviolet made inside an energy efficient lamp is invisible and why a sunbed can burn skin that feels nothing unusual.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Infrared can be seen – it is the red glow you see from a heater or a grill.
items.correct: Infrared is invisible; the red glow is visible light that the very hot element also emits.
items.misconception: The red colour of a hot element is the infrared radiation itself.
items.why: The word 'infrared' contains 'red', and the two are emitted together by anything hot enough to glow, so the visible glow is taken as proof that infrared is visible. A heater that is not glowing at all still emits plenty of infrared, and an infrared camera detects people who give out no visible light. Infrared lies beyond red, at wavelengths the eye cannot detect.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Ultraviolet from a sunbed is safe, because the exposure is short and controlled.
items.correct: Ultraviolet from a sunbed can damage skin cells however it is delivered.
items.misconception: A controlled indoor dose of ultraviolet carries no risk.
items.why: Sunbeds are sold as a managed alternative to the sun, and the risk from sunlight is presented as a sunburn risk, so an indoor lamp with a timer feels harmless. It is the ultraviolet itself that is absorbed by skin cells, and the source makes no difference. The specification lists sun tanning as an application of ultraviolet while treating that radiation as one that can harm skin.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: An X-ray image is formed by X-rays bouncing off the bone back to the film.
items.correct: The image is a shadow made by X-rays that have passed through the body.
items.misconception: X-rays reflect from bone the way light reflects from a mirror.
items.why: Ordinary photography works by reflected light, so students carry the same model across to X-rays without asking whether the radiation goes through the patient. The detector is on the far side of the patient from the X-ray tube. What reaches it is the radiation that got through, so dense bone leaves a pale shadow while soft tissue leaves a darker region.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Gamma rays are far too dangerous to be used on a person for any reason.
items.correct: Gamma rays are used in hospitals to treat cancer, with the beam carefully directed and the dose controlled.
items.misconception: Because gamma rays are hazardous, they can have no medical use.
items.why: Gamma rays are taught first as the most penetrating and most dangerous radiation, so the hazard is remembered and the controlled application is not. The specification pairs X-rays and gamma rays with medical imaging and treatments. The same property that makes gamma rays hazardous – their ability to damage cells – is what allows a directed beam to kill the cells of a tumour.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Infrared cannot travel through empty space, because it needs something to carry the heat.
items.correct: Infrared is an electromagnetic wave and travels through a vacuum, but it is strongly absorbed by the atmosphere.
items.misconception: Infrared needs a medium, so it cannot cross the vacuum between the earth and a satellite.
items.why: Infrared is met as a way of transferring energy from hot objects, alongside conduction and convection, which do need a medium. Infrared from the Sun crosses 150 million kilometres of vacuum to reach us. The reason microwaves rather than infrared are used for satellite links is that the atmosphere transmits microwaves while it absorbs much of the infrared.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Any invisible radiation that is used to send or detect something can be called radio waves.
items.correct: Each group of the spectrum has its own applications; 'radio waves' names one group only.
items.misconception: Radio waves are the general name for invisible radiation.
items.why: Radio waves are the first group met, and everyday language uses 'radio' loosely for any wireless signal, so the term expands to cover the whole invisible spectrum. The spectrum is divided into named groups by wavelength, and the specification gives each its own applications: radio waves for television and radio, microwaves for satellite links and microwave ovens, X-rays and gamma rays for medical imaging.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A bone shows up on an X-ray because it gives out light of its own when the X-rays hit it.
items.correct: The bone absorbs X-rays and casts a shadow on the detector.
items.misconception: The bone is made to glow, and the image records that glow.
items.why: The finished image looks like a photograph of something bright, so students invent a source inside the body rather than picturing a shadow. No radiation is emitted by the bone. X-rays from the tube pass through the patient; bone absorbs most of them, so fewer arrive behind it and that region of the image stays pale.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Gamma rays are only ever used to take pictures inside the body.
items.correct: X-rays and gamma rays are used both for medical imaging and for treatments.
items.misconception: Imaging is the only medical use of these waves.
items.why: Imaging is the use students meet first and can picture, and the word 'ray' is tied to X-ray photographs, so treatment is forgotten. The specification names both uses: medical imaging and treatments. In treatment a beam of gamma rays is directed at a tumour so that the cells absorbing it are destroyed.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If there is a clear line of sight to something, visible light is used to send the signal.
items.correct: Satellite links use microwaves, even though there is a clear path to the satellite.
items.misconception: A straight, unobstructed path means the signal must be carried by light.
items.why: Light is the wave students know travels in straight lines, so line of sight is taken as evidence that light is being used. All electromagnetic waves travel in straight lines through a uniform medium. The wave chosen for a link depends on what the atmosphere transmits and what the equipment can send and detect, which is why satellite communications use microwaves and fibre optics use visible light.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.6.2.4 Uses and applications of electromagnetic waves
